extracted.intended_audience: students and practitioners of public relations; communications managers
extracted.subtask_description: Standards and evaluative criteria for public relations practice across specialties (public affairs, lobbying, issues management, crisis management, investor relations, development) as presented in a public relations textbook chapter. Emphasizes functions, qualifications, processes, ethics, and managerial expectations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Public affairs definition and scope
rubrics_metrics.description: “Public affairs is the public relations practice that addresses public policy and the publics who influence such policy.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Public affairs includes activities related to public policy, corporate citizenship, and CSR; titles include public affairs, public information, community relations, liaison, corporate affairs, government relations, external affairs. Responsibilities (surveyed) include federal, state, and local government affairs, community relations, political action committees, contributions, grassroots support, and issues management. Public affairs specialists act as liaisons with governmental units and implement community improvement programs. Emphasizes honest and transparent communications and navigating governmental processes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Public affairs specialist qualifications and tasks
rubrics_metrics.description: Job requirements and duties for public affairs managers as described in the example job description.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Preferred qualifications: B.A. combining public relations and political science, ~5 years corporate–government relations experience; graduate work or law degree a plus; strong oral and written communication skills; knowledge of local government and public sector regulatory processes; some media experience. Typical duties: develop/implement public affairs programs, monitor franchise compliance, lead media relations, produce press materials, conduct community relations programs, work with district managers and top management. Guidance implies that practical knowledge of political processes and strong communications skills are evaluative criteria for hiring and performance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Lobbying: definition and legal/ethical framework
rubrics_metrics.description: Lobbying is defined as “the practice of trying to persuade legislators to propose, pass, or defeat legislation or to change existing laws.” It is the specialized part of public relations that builds and maintains relations with government to influence legislation and regulation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Legal requirements: anyone lobbying U.S. Congress must register with the Clerk of the House and Secretary of the Senate; failure to register can carry fines (up to $50,000 under the Lobbying Disclosure Act of 1995); semiannual reports of clients, expenditures, and issue-related activities required. Ethical concerns: distinguish open advocacy from manipulation; avoid deceptive practices (e.g., astroturf). Practical requirements: deep knowledge of legislative process, government functions, and relationships with lawmakers/officials; often staffed by former government insiders or lawyers. Lobbying should be coordinated with broader PR efforts, mobilize constituents (grassroots), and use modern tools (email, social media) while maintaining credibility and transparency.

rubrics_metrics.name: Lobbyist principal activities
rubrics_metrics.description: Quotation enumerating principal elements of lobbying work.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Key activities: researching and analyzing legislation or regulatory proposals; monitoring and reporting on developments; attending congressional or regulatory hearings; working with coalitions interested in the same issues; educating government officials as well as employees and corporate officers about implications of changes. Note that direct communication with officials is only a small portion of time; preparation, information, and communication comprise the larger workload. This list functions as an operational rubric for evaluating lobbying thoroughness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Grassroots vs astroturf ethical distinction
rubrics_metrics.description: Use of grassroots lobbying to mobilize constituents versus deceptive 'front' groups ('Astroturf lobbying') created to mislead policymakers about public sentiment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Grassroots lobbying: mobilize genuine constituents via mail, phone, email, social media, and other tools. Anti-pattern: creating faux grassroots 'front' groups to fabricate public support—examples include groups funded by interested sponsors to mask narrow interests. Evaluative criterion: authenticity and transparency of constituency mobilization.

rubrics_metrics.name: Issues management core definition
rubrics_metrics.description: “Issues management is the process of anticipating, identifying, evaluating, and responding to issues and trends that potentially affect an organization’s relationships with its publics.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Essence captured in two points: (1) early identification of issues with potential impact on an organization and (2) a strategic response designed to mitigate or capitalize on their consequences. Issues management seeks to discern trends in public opinion so the organization can respond before they amplify into serious conflict. Use for evaluation: timeliness of detection, quality of analysis, prioritization, chosen strategies, implementation, and evaluation of outcomes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Issues management process steps
rubrics_metrics.description: Steps as originally conceived and later expanded by experts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Typical process: identifying issues, analyzing issues, setting priorities, selecting program strategies, implementing programs of action and communication, and evaluating effectiveness. Expanded panel definition: anticipating, researching and prioritizing issues; assessing impact; recommending policies/strategies to minimize risk and seize opportunities; participating in and implementing strategy; evaluating program impact. Anti-patterns: treating issues management solely as manipulative persuasive communication rather than aligning organizational actions with stakeholder expectations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Crisis management definition
rubrics_metrics.description: “Crisis management is the public relations specialty that helps organizations strategically respond to negative situations and to dialog with stakeholders affected by perceived and actual consequences of crises.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Crisis management is invoked when issues management fails to prevent a serious event. Emphasizes strategic response, dialogue with stakeholders, and protection/recovery of reputation. Practical expectations include preparedness, rapid coordinated decision-making, and senior management involvement. Crisis specialists should combine planning, communication skills, and an understanding of legal and reputational risks.

rubrics_metrics.name: Crisis management stages (Coombs & Fearn-Banks)
rubrics_metrics.description: Coombs: three macrostages—precrisis, crisis, postcrisis. Fearn-Banks: five stages—(1) detection, (2) prevention/preparation, (3) containment, (4) recovery, and (5) learning.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Precrisis: detect, prevent, prepare. Crisis: respond to trigger event, contain damage, recover. Postcrisis: activities after crisis (learning, change). The 'learning' phase should bring organizational change to help prevent future crises. Practical rubric: presence of plans for each stage, rehearsal, defined decision authorities, and postcrisis evaluation leading to policy changes. Researchers note no single strategy fits all situations; maintaining good relationships is often the best approach.

rubrics_metrics.name: Investor relations definition and goals
rubrics_metrics.description: Investor relations (IR) is 'the specialized part of corporate public relations that builds and maintains mutually beneficial relationships with shareholders and others in the financial community to maximize market value.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Goals: enhance stock value, reduce cost of capital by increasing shareholder confidence and making stock attractive to analysts and institutional investors. Activities: tracking market trends, monitoring financial blogs and social networks, providing information to financial publics, counseling management, responding to information requests. Methods for dissemination: annual/quarterly reports, SEC 10-K forms, emailed earnings reports, press releases via newswires, website links to material financial information.

rubrics_metrics.name: Investor relations required expertise
rubrics_metrics.description: IR practitioners must know corporate finance, accounting, Wall Street, international equities trading, business journalism, SEC and stock-exchange reporting requirements.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because of required technical skills, public relations graduates without finance/accounting training may not be competitive for IR roles. Recommended preparation includes combining PR studies with finance/business law coursework; MBA often necessary. Evaluative criterion: technical competence in finance and regulatory reporting, language skills, international awareness, and ability to manage investor communications effectively.

rubrics_metrics.name: Development (fundraising and membership) definition
rubrics_metrics.description: Development is 'the specialized part of public relations in nonprofit organizations that builds and maintains relationships with donors, volunteers, and members to secure financial and volunteer support.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Activities include annual campaigns, telethons, fundraising events (10K runs, auctions), membership services, volunteer recruitment, and long-term relationship-building. Because nonprofits rely on donations and volunteer time, development programs are central to organizational survival. Evaluative criteria: effectiveness of solicitation programs, event management, donor relations, retention, and integration with organizational goals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Confusion of terms and organizational labeling
rubrics_metrics.description: Many organizations use varied labels (public relations, public affairs, public information, corporate relations, corporate communication, university advancement, hospital relations) to describe similar functions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Despite differing titles, the basic concept and motivation—establishing and maintaining relationships with important publics—is similar. Evaluative emphasis: clarity of role, integration with other functions, whether PR is narrowly defined (e.g., product publicity) or embraced as strategic management. Anti-pattern: employers/clients defining PR narrowly or incorrectly, isolating it from senior management and organizational strategy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Senior management responsibility and support
rubrics_metrics.description: An organization’s relationships are the responsibility of top management; public relations 'is the boss’s job to build and keep strong bonds with key groups.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: PR success requires senior management support and cooperation and cannot be isolated from other operations. Evaluative measures: direct reporting lines to senior leadership, management involvement in PR decisions, and alignment of PR with strategic management goals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Core axiom 1: Broad view of environment
rubrics_metrics.description: Public relations takes a broad view of an organization’s environment by attending to a wide range of issues and relationships with stakeholders.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate PR by how comprehensively it scans and responds to relevant environmental factors, stakeholders, and issues beyond narrow media relations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Core axiom 2: Part of strategic management
rubrics_metrics.description: Public relations is part of strategic management, seeking to avoid or solve problems through a goal-directed process.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess PR by its integration into strategy-setting and problem-solving, not merely as reactive communication.

rubrics_metrics.name: Core axiom 3: Outcomes must be quantified and measured
rubrics_metrics.description: Public relations outcomes must be quantified and measured. This requires a detailed understanding and assessment of what’s happening now and of desired future states.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluative criterion: presence of measurable objectives, baseline assessments, metrics, and evaluation plans tied to desired outcomes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Core axiom 4: Strategic planning begins with situation analysis
rubrics_metrics.description: Strategic planning begins by identifying the current conditions motivating the process, the contributing forces and actors in the situation, the objectives to be achieved with each target public, and the overall program goal.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess quality of planning by clarity of situation analysis, stakeholder mapping, specific objectives per public, and coherent overall goals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Core axiom 5: Programs outline path from current to desired state
rubrics_metrics.description: Public relations programs outline how the organization will get from where it is to where it wants to be.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate programs by the clarity and feasibility of tactics, timelines, responsibilities, and indicators of progress.

rubrics_metrics.name: Core axiom 6: Requires senior management support
rubrics_metrics.description: Public relations initiatives must have senior management’s support and cooperation, and cannot be isolated from other operations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Duplicate of managerial responsibility axiom but listed to emphasize that PR effectiveness depends on organizational buy-in and cross-departmental coordination.

rubrics_metrics.name: Core axiom 7: Actions matter more than words
rubrics_metrics.description: Success or failure depends more on what the organization does than on what it says, unless the communication itself becomes a problem.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluative focus: alignment between organizational behavior and communications; avoid token messaging that lacks corresponding action. Success requires coordinated deeds and words.

rubrics_metrics.name: Core axiom 8: Ethics, legality, and social responsibility
rubrics_metrics.description: Success also requires that all actions, communication, and outcomes are ethical, legal, and consistent with the organization’s social responsibility.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluation should include legal compliance, ethical standards, CSR alignment, and the reputational implications of tactics (e.g., avoid astroturf, deceptive practices).

rubrics_metrics.name: Core axiom 9: Impact on society and culture
rubrics_metrics.description: Ultimately, success is based on the organization’s impact on society and culture—as is the character and professional careers of the public relations practitioners who helped plan and implement its programs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess long-term societal effects and the ethical legacy of PR programs; consider broader cultural consequences and practitioner's professional integrity.
